stem: The waxy thick layer that often covers the outside of the epidermis and prevents the loss of water is called the
options: Casparian strip
Hypodermis
Bundle sheath
Cuticle
explanation: Correct option: (D). The outside of the epidermis is often covered by a waxy thick layer, the cuticle, which prevents water loss; it is absent in roots. Casparian strips are suberin bands on endodermal walls of the root, the hypodermis is a layer of the cortex just below the epidermis, and the bundle sheath surrounds vascular bundles.

stem: In grasses, the guard cells that enclose the stomatal pore are
options: Bean-shaped
Dumb-bell shaped
Crescent-shaped
Barrel-shaped cells
explanation: Correct option: (B). Each stoma normally has two bean-shaped guard cells, but in grasses the guard cells are dumb-bell shaped. stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes root hairs from the trichomes of the shoot?
options: Root hairs are unicellular and absorb water; trichomes are usually multicellular and cut water loss.
Root hairs are multicellular and secretory; trichomes are unicellular and absorb minerals from soil.
Both are unicellular outgrowths of cortical cells that absorb water and minerals from the soil.
Root hairs are covered by a thick cuticle; trichomes are always soft, unbranched and non-secretory.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Root hairs are unicellular elongations of epidermal cells that absorb water and minerals; trichomes on the shoot are usually multicellular and help prevent water loss by transpiration. Root hairs are not multicellular, both structures arise from the epidermis and not the cortex, roots have no cuticle, and trichomes may be branched, stiff or secretory.

stem: The epidermis of the shoot is often covered by a cuticle, but the cuticle is absent in roots. Which reason best explains why this absence suits the root?
options: Roots exchange gases only through their stomata, which a waxy cuticle would block.
Root epidermal cells have no vacuole, so they are unable to secrete any waxy material.
A waxy, water-proof layer would hinder the uptake of water and minerals by the root.
A cuticle is needed only on cells that contain chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis.
explanation: Correct option: (C). The cuticle prevents the loss of water because it is waxy and water-proof; on a root, whose epidermis and root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil, such a layer would block absorption. Roots do not have stomata (stomata are present in the epidermis of leaves), epidermal cells have a large vacuole, and the cuticle is not linked to chloroplasts since it also covers non-green stem epidermis.

Medullary rays
Bundle sheath

stem: Which one of the following is NOT a part of the ground tissue system of a primary dicot root?
options: Endodermis
Pericycle
Epiblema
Pith
explanation: Correct option: (C). All tissues except the epidermis and the vascular bundles form the ground tissue, which is divided into cortex, pericycle and pith. The epiblema is the outermost (epidermal) layer of the root, so it belongs to the epidermal tissue system. The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex, and the pericycle and pith are also ground tissue.

stem: In a section, each vascular bundle has xylem and phloem on the same radius, phloem only on the outer side, and a strip of cambium between them. What can be concluded about these bundles?
options: They are radial and open, as is typical of the primary root of a dicot.
They are conjoint and closed, so no secondary tissue can ever be formed.
They are conjoint and open, as is typical of the vascular bundles of a monocot stem.
They are conjoint and open, so they can form secondary xylem and phloem.
explanation: Correct option: (D). Xylem and phloem on the same radius make the bundle conjoint; cambium between them makes it open, and an open bundle can form secondary xylem and phloem, as in dicot stems. Radial bundles have xylem and phloem on different radii; a bundle with cambium is not closed; and monocot stem bundles lack cambium, so they are closed, not open.

stem: A transverse section of a root shows about eight xylem patches alternating with phloem, a large and well developed pith, and no cambium. The section is most likely of a
options: Monocot root, which is polyarch and has a large pith
Dicot root, which has many xylem bundles and a small pith
Monocot stem, which has scattered conjoint closed bundles
Dicot root that has completed its secondary growth
explanation: Correct option: (A). Alternating xylem and phloem (radial bundles) show it is a root. More than six xylem bundles (polyarch), a large well developed pith and no secondary growth are features of the monocot root. A dicot root usually has two to four xylem patches and a small pith; a monocot stem has conjoint, scattered bundles, not radial ones; and a dicot root after secondary growth would show a cambium ring and secondary tissues.

stem: The endodermal cells of a sunflower root are barrel-shaped, have no intercellular spaces, and carry water-impermeable suberin as casparian strips on their radial and tangential walls. Which inference is best supported by these features?
options: The endodermis stores starch grains and acts as the starch sheath of the root.
The endodermis is the layer that gives rise to lateral roots in the mature root.
The endodermis forms the outer limit of the conjunctive tissue between bundles.
Water cannot seep inward through the walls or the gaps between endodermal cells.
explanation: Correct option: (D). With no intercellular spaces and water-impermeable suberin on the radial and tangential walls, water cannot pass inward through the endodermal walls or between its cells. Calling the endodermis a starch sheath describes the dicot stem, lateral roots arise from the pericycle, and conjunctive tissue lies between xylem and phloem inside the stele, not at the endodermis.

options: Its walls carry suberin casparian strips
It forms semi-lunar patches over phloem

stem: Which combination of features would identify a section as that of a monocot stem?
options: Collenchymatous hypodermis, ring of open bundles, medullary rays
Sclerenchymatous hypodermis, radial bundles and a large pith
Parenchymatous hypodermis, scattered open bundles, starch sheath
Sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered closed sheathed bundles
explanation: Correct option: (D). A monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis and a large number of scattered, conjoint, closed vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath. A collenchymatous hypodermis with a ring of open bundles and medullary rays is a dicot stem; radial bundles occur in roots; and monocot stem bundles are closed, not open.

stem: Read the case about stems P and Q. Which conclusion about the two stems is correct?
options: P is a monocot stem, because its bundles are separated by medullary rays.
Q is a monocot stem whose bundles are closed and cannot add secondary tissue.
Q is a dicot stem, because its central bundles are larger than its outer ones.
P is a monocot stem, because cambium is seen between its xylem and phloem.
explanation: Correct option: (B). Q has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths, no phloem parenchyma, water-containing cavities and smaller peripheral bundles, all features of a monocot stem; its bundles lack cambium, so they are closed and form no secondary tissue. P, with a collenchymatous hypodermis, a ring of bundles, medullary rays and cambium (open bundles), is a dicot stem. Larger central bundles are in fact a monocot feature, not a dicot one.

stem: In a dorsiventral leaf, the palisade parenchyma consists of
options: Loose oval cells extending to the lower epidermis
Colourless empty cells along the upper epidermis
Elongated adaxial cells, vertical and parallel
Thick-walled cells forming a sheath round bundles

stem: Bulliform cells, found in the leaves of grasses, are
options: Chloroplast-rich palisade cells below the upper epidermis
Dumb-bell shaped guard cells found on both leaf surfaces
Thick-walled bundle sheath cells around the main veins
Large, empty, colourless adaxial epidermal cells by veins

Reason (R): In an isobilateral leaf, stomata are present only on the abaxial (lower) epidermis.

stem: On a hot afternoon, under water stress, the leaves of a grass curl inwards. What explains this?
options: Bulliform cells turn flaccid, so the leaf curls and loses less water
Bulliform cells turn turgid, so the leaf folds and exposes more surface
Guard cells lose their chloroplasts, so the stomata close permanently
Palisade cells swell with water and push both leaf margins inwards
explanation: Correct option: (A). When bulliform cells have absorbed water and are turgid, the leaf surface is exposed; when they become flaccid due to water stress, the leaves curl inwards to minimise water loss. Turgid bulliform cells keep the leaf open rather than curled, guard cells do not lose chloroplasts, and the mesophyll of a grass leaf is not differentiated into palisade cells.

stem: A vertical section of a leaf shows more stomata on the lower surface than on the upper, mesophyll differentiated into two kinds of cells, and vascular bundles of clearly different sizes. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: It is isobilateral, since bundles of varying size reflect parallel venation.
It is dorsiventral, since unequal bundle sizes reflect reticulate venation.
It is isobilateral, since its stomata occur on both of the leaf surfaces.
It is dorsiventral, since its mesophyll shows no differentiation at all.
explanation: Correct option: (B). More stomata on the abaxial surface and mesophyll differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma mark a dorsiventral (dicot) leaf; the size of the bundles depends on the size of the veins, which vary in thickness in reticulate venation. Parallel venation gives bundles of nearly similar size, the section does not show equal stomata on both surfaces, and a dorsiventral leaf does have differentiated mesophyll.
